pages.x: When King Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066, three men claimed England: Harold Godwinson, the richest earl, crowned the next day; Harald Hardrada, king of Norway; and William, Duke of Normandy, who said Edward had promised him the crown, and Harold had sworn to help him get it.

Hardrada struck first, landing in Yorkshire in September. King Harold marched north in days and took him by surprise at Stamford Bridge, near York. Hardrada was killed by an arrow in the throat. Of some 300 ships that had come, 24 were enough to carry the survivors home.

William had waited weeks for a south wind. It came two days after Stamford Bridge. He landed unopposed at Pevensey with perhaps 7,000 men and their horses, and put up a wooden castle. Harold raced south again.

On 14 October Harold's army formed a shield wall on a ridge near Hastings. All day the Norman knights charged uphill. Twice they pretended to flee, drawing English soldiers down the slope. By evening Harold was dead, by tradition with an arrow in the eye.

William was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066. Outside, Norman guards heard the shouts of acclaim, thought it was a riot and set fire to nearby houses. For years the English kept rising against him.

When the north rose again in 1069, William had villages, crops and cattle destroyed from York to Durham, so that famine would finish the rebels. A chronicler of the next century said 100,000 people died.

pages.x: A strip of embroidered linen almost 70 metres long tells the Norman side of the story, from Harold's oath to the battle, like a comic strip: ships, horses, Halley's comet, and a soldier gripping an arrow in his eye.
The Normans held England down with hundreds of castles, first of earth and timber, then of stone, such as the White Tower in London.
pages.fx: In 1086 William had every estate recorded, with its land, people, ploughs and pigs, in the Domesday Book, so complete it was named after Judgement Day.

pages.x: The conquest replaced England's rulers with French-speaking Normans and tied England to France for centuries. It changed English itself: thousands of French words, such as beef, pork, justice and parliament, came into the language.
